Design elements — reference

Confirmed elements to carry forward. Added one at a time.

FOR THE DEVELOPER — BUILD SPEC, READ FIRST
This document contains many exploratory variants of the same components, kept for the record. Only the following are approved for build:

Button: RCW2F — flush inlay construction, felt-marked paper (section 14) at reduced texture, sans label, soft shadow. Marked final inside the button gallery, Element 16. Do not use any other button code (BLU/GRN/RED/WPS/WPG/SLA/SLB/SLC/RCS/RCW/RCB/RCW2/RCW2R, etc.) — those are earlier steps in the process, not options to pick from.

Waitlist card: Element 20, marked final. Element 21 uses the RCW2R button and was the client's rejected alternative — marked not selected, kept for reference only.

Postpartum Suite - Press

In the weeks after birth your body is doing something enormous and quiet. You are sore. You are not sleeping. You are learning a new person from scratch, often at three in the morning, often alone.

And somewhere in the middle of it, the meals stop being cooked, the washing piles up, and the last thing that gets attention is you.

Four kinds of care, every day

She is there for the practical and the invisible. Settling and soothing, nappies, bathing, and taking the night shift so you can have an unbroken stretch of sleep.

One 1024px greyscale tile, seamless, midtone normalised to 128.
141 KB as WebP. Applied through a pseudo-element so three things
stay adjustable independently:

--c  paper colour   any colour. the texture is luminance only,
                    so hue is never baked in
--s  grain scale    FIXED PIXELS, never a percentage. real paper
                    fibre is a physical constant, so it must not
                    scale with the viewport
--o  strength       0 to 1

mix-blend-mode: soft-light;

Authored at 1024 and shown at 512 css px, which covers 2x retina.
One asset can serve every elevation: same tile, different scale
and strength gives base sheet, card stock and pressed well.

  RCS1  cut out and inlaid, flush with the sheet
        no elevation at all: no cast shadow, no inset well. A
        groove needs a light and a dark wall, and a wall only
        exists if one surface sits above or below the other. Card
        and sheet sit at the same level, so the only shading is
        one thin, uniform seam at the cut.

        Label is now CRM1's plain treatment, not the enlarged
        lbl-lg lbl-soft version, 16px with the -webkit-text-stroke
        synthetic weight.

        Texture pushed hard, since with no shadow doing the work
        of separating the two materials, contrast has to carry
        more of it. Contrast raised from 10.5 to 26.0, tile
        dropped from 420px to 280px so more of the pattern shows
        across the button's width, opacity to 1.

  RCS2  RCS1 in blue #93A7B8
  RCS3  RCS1 in green #9FAE8C
        Same face, seam and kerf recipe as RCS1, colours pulled
        from CSS variables rather than duplicated CSS, so the
        seam tint follows the card's own hue instead of staying
        a fixed brown on every colour.

Mix freely, for example "WRS1 surface on GRN1 colour".
STRUCTURE  edge 11px → groove → 4px → groove → 15px → text
RADIUS     5px, up from 3px

THICKNESS  halved. two lines instead of four
  0 1px 0   rgba(181,162,135,0.85)
  0 2px 1px rgba(160,141,115,0.65)

TOP EDGE   two things stop it vanishing into the sheet
  0 0 0 1px rgba(120,98,74,0.07)        faint silhouette
  inset 0 1px 0 rgba(253,247,235,0.55)  lit top face
  and the board colour lifted to #EDE4D8 against the
  #E2D7C6 sheet, so there is a tonal step as well

SURFACE    two layers now, which is where the mottling
           comes from
  mottled cartridge  1000px, soft-light, contrast 15.0
  hammered           420px,  soft-light, contrast 10.0
  Both pulled back from 33.4 and 22.0, which were fighting
  the button rather than supporting it.

HIGHLIGHTS  every one reduced by about 40 percent and
            warmed further off white

LABEL  ink on the blue measures 6.96:1, so contrast was
       never the issue. The deboss highlight was eating into
       the letterform edge and thinning it.
  16px current      the baseline
  19px + 0.55px stroke, tracking 0.14em
  19px + deboss cut to a single faint line
  19px + soft gold foil #D6B67C, struck in

BLUES  ink contrast against each
  #93A7B8  6.96:1   passes everywhere
  #6E8CA8  4.92:1   passes
  #4A6E92  3.24:1   fails normal text, passes as large text
                    only. foil or a cream label would fix it.

WHITE  #F3F7FB on #4A6E92 is 4.96:1, so a white label
       solves that contrast problem outright.
WHY THEY LOOKED IDENTICAL
  -webkit-text-stroke draws in the glyph's own colour. A white
  stroke at 0.55px was adding white on all four sides and
  burying the 1px shadows underneath it. Cut to 0.25px.

AND THREE REAL DIFFERENCES, NOT JUST SWAPPED OFFSETS
  glyph colour  deboss #D7E4F0 dimmer, light cannot reach the
                bottom of a groove
                emboss #FCFDFF brighter than the card's white,
                the top face catches the most light
  offsets       1.5px, up from 1px
  cast shadow   emboss throws 3px 4px 5px onto the card.
                deboss has none. a hole does not cast a shadow.
                that is the strongest signal of the two.

SILHOUETTE ring reduced from 0.15 to 0.07

COLOUR  every tone is a variable, so a swatch sets --face
        plus its edge, groove, highlight and cast shadow tints.
        The texture files never change. They are greyscale
        luminance, so colour is never baked in.
  green #9FAE8C   blue #93A7B8   red #B98A7E

Dropping hammered from 768px to 420px means the button now
shows nearly two tiles across rather than a third of one,
which is what was hiding the texture.
17

Mounting a photograph

real assets · texture never touches the photo pixels

1 · Flush, no mountthe card's own shadow is the frame

2 · Flush, inlaid seamRCS1's own kerf, same photo as option 3

3 · Ridged frame, gappedelement 18's raised separator, as a border

4 · Depressed above and belowboth lines debossed

5 · Ridged above and belowboth lines embossed

6 · Ridged, either sidevertical only, no top or bottom

7 · Depressed, either sidevertical only, no top or bottom

8 · Ridged, closed loop11 and 12 combined, four bars meeting at the corners

9 · Depressed, closed loopsame construction as 14, debossed instead of embossed

THE RULE  no blend mode, no texture, ever sits directly over
        the photo's own pixels. It would colour cast and degrade
        the image. Texture applies only to the mount around it.
        The img element itself is always untouched, full resolution.

1 · FLUSH  no separate border. The raised card edge is
        the only frame. Quietest option, best in a grid of several
        photos where an ornate mount on each would compete.

2 · INLAID SEAM  the button's own RCS1 technique. No
        texture layer, since blending anything onto the photo's
        pixels is the one rule that never bends, so this is
        simpler than the button: just the img, and the same
        kerf-roughened 0.75px seam at its own edge.

3 · RIDGED FRAME  a real offset shadow spans the whole
        box so its direction is correct, then a mask repaints
        everything except the outer ~2px with a fresh copy of the
        sheet's own texture, physically covering the shadow inside
        that boundary. Only a thin line at the very edge of the
        frame can ever show any shading. 14px gap before it.

4 · BANDED, DEPRESSED
5 · BANDED, RIDGED
        Element 18's separator classes, unchanged, placed directly
        above and below the photo. No frame, no left or right edge,
        since a line only ever needs one direction to be correct.
        14px gap, 16px overhang beyond the photo on each side.

6 · RIDGED, EITHER SIDE
7 · DEPRESSED, EITHER SIDE
        The same idea as 4 and 5, rotated. A vertical line's wall
        faces left or right instead of up or down, so the shadow
        moves from the y-axis to the x-axis. Same 14px gap, same
        16px overhang, now top and bottom instead of either side.

8 · RIDGED, CLOSED LOOP
9 · DEPRESSED, CLOSED LOOP
        4/5 and 6/7 combined. Four independent bars, the exact
        separator recipes, unchanged, sized so their ends meet at
        the corners. Both axes use the same 14px value for the gap
        and the overhang, which is what makes the corners meet
        precisely. No shared background, no shadow spanning the
        interior, nothing describing a plane, so this does not
        carry the platform reading the earlier closed-rectangle
        attempts had. Four lines that happen to touch, not one
        shape drawn around the photo.
18

Separators

drawn · debossed · embossed

1 · Drawn — flat ink, no shadow at all

She is there for the practical and the invisible, settling and soothing, taking the night shift so you can sleep.

The washing moves quietly through the day, folded and put away before you notice it needed doing.

2 · Debossed — pressed into the paper, tight edges

She is there for the practical and the invisible, settling and soothing, taking the night shift so you can sleep.

Meals are cooked fresh in your own kitchen, warming and simple, timed around when you actually want to eat.

3 · Embossed — raised off the paper, diffuse cast shadow

She is there for the practical and the invisible, settling and soothing, taking the night shift so you can sleep.

Treatments happen daily rather than as a single occasion, a small part of every day rather than a one-off.

1 · DRAWN
  height: 1px;
  background: rgba(30,26,22,0.38);
  No shadow at all. Ink sitting flat on the page, same logic as
  body text, the plainest of the three.

2 · DEBOSSED
  background: rgba(52,38,26,0.32);
  box-shadow: 0 1px 0 rgba(250,243,229,0.55);
  Zero blur on the light edge. A groove's walls are tight against
  each other, which is the rule this whole document has used
  throughout: tight equals pressed.

3 · EMBOSSED
  background: rgba(250,243,229,0.62);
  box-shadow: 0 2px 3px rgba(52,38,26,0.28);
  Blurred, offset cast shadow instead of a tight edge. A raised
  ridge throws a real shadow onto the surface below it, and that
  shadow spreads the way any cast shadow does. Diffuse equals
  raised, the same principle in reverse.

A separator only needs one direction, so neither of these runs
into the problem the button's four-sided seam had. One dark side,
one light side, is enough to read correctly on its own.

Debossed logo mark

TSB FAVACON.png · laid/ribbed paper, element 13's settings 
SOURCE   TSB FAVACON.png, 800x800. Ink isolated by luminance,
        background cream and transparent margin dropped, leaving
        only the circle stroke and the "tps" script as an alpha
        mask, cropped tight and re-exported at 480px.

PAPER    laid/ribbed, element 13's own locked settings
        --c:#E2D7C6  --s:320px  --o:0.85

PRESS    filter: url(#letterpress), the same filter used
        on elements 02 and 04, unchanged. feTurbulence for fibre,
        feDisplacementMap to rough the edge, feSpecularLighting
        with a negative surfaceScale to press it in, lit from the
        same upper-left direction as everything else on the page.

FILL     #16110C, the same dark ink used everywhere else
        pressed text appears on this page. The earlier blind
        deboss, paper coloured with no separate ink, put almost
        no contrast between the fill and the specular highlight,
        which is why the depth was invisible rather than subtle.

REBUILT  filter and drop-shadow abandoned for this
        element. drop-shadow() runs on the source shape and the
        mask clips the result after, in some browsers, so it may
        well have been shadowing a plain rectangle rather than the
        logo, which explains why scaling the numbers up still did
        nothing.

THREE LAYERS  the same principle as text-shadow, built
        by hand instead of relying on a filter to fake it:
          ld-shadow  #050301, translate(-0.6px,-0.6px), blur 0.5px
          ld-light   #FBF3E3, translate(0.6px,0.6px),   blur 0.5px
          ld-main    #16110C, no offset
        The stroke width at this display size is only a pixel or
        two, so the first attempt at 3px pushed both copies clear
        of the main line entirely, reading as parallel outlines
        rather than a shaded edge. Pulled back to a fraction of a
        pixel and softened with a touch of blur, so what shows is
        a faint dark and light fringe blending into the stroke's
        own edge rather than a second line sitting beside it.

        when forced onto a centre axis.
